newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Rebel resistance slows Sri Lanka army push.
newsitem.headline: Rebel resistance slows Sri Lanka army push.

text.p: Sri Lankan forces reported slow progress in their pincer offensive on Tamil Tiger guerrillas' northern stronghold on Thursday, which analysts said proved the rebels' strength.
Military officials said the army, backed by strikes from air force bombers and artillery, moved closer to the northern rebel stronghold of Kilinochchi, 285 km (180 miles) north of Colombo.

A military spokeman said two columns of troops made progress in their advance from the road junction town of Paranthan, six km (four miles) north of Kilinochchi, approaching the rebel base from different directions.

"On the western flank, troops captured one important road junction by yesterday afternoon," the spokesman said. "Terrorists offered heavy resistance during this confrontaton in which 13 soldiers were killed and 30 wounded."

This brings the death toll for the army to 71 and the number of wounded to 145 in fighting near Kilinochchi since Sunday when the government launched the offensive after more than a month's lull in the conflict.

The military spokesman said the troops continued to dominate the newly captured area in fighting on its eastern flank, but rebel resistance, using mortars, rocket-propelled grenades and automatic rifles, limited army progress to one km (half a mile) overnight.
"Later reports indicate that terrorists launched a massive counter-attack during the very early hours of today," he said of the fighting on the western flank.
"It was effectively repulsed. The troops effectively caused heavy casualties among terrorists," he said without giving figures.

Military analysts and diplomats said that despite claims by government forces of heavy rebel casualties, their assault launched four days ago again displayed the sharp claws of the separatist Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE).
"Normally, for an operation like this, one would have expected it to end in half a day because of proximity," military commentator Iqbal Athas told Reuters.
"The bottom line is that they are meeting very hard resistance," said Athas who writes for the local Sunday Times newspaper.
The military has been targeting Kilinochchi since the Tigers overran the northeastern Mullaitivu camp in July, killing or capturing almost its entire garrison of well over 1,000 men.
The defeat, which dramatically demonstrated rebel strength, was the military's worst setback in the 13-year war, in which the government says more than 50,000 people have died.

The government took the upper hand earlier this year when the Tigers lost their stronghold of the northernmost Jaffna peninsula, which they had ruled for almost a decade with their own administration, courts and police.
The rebels want an independent homeland in the island's north and east.
Defence Ministry officials have said several army divisions taking part in the assault either killed or wounded more than 500 rebels in the first three days of the fighting.
But army sources said radio communications by the LTTE and monitored by the military said only 61 guerrillas, including 23 officers, were killed.
"The emphasis has always been laid on the death by the military in their propaganda," an Asian diplomat said. "I would put the real toll in between the two claims."
